newsitem.title: UK: Sterling, darling of the market, where to now?.
newsitem.headline: Sterling, darling of the market, where to now?.

text.p: Sterling surged anew after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke sprang a quarter point interest rate rise on the markets.
For the pound it was more a treat than a trick. It romped up to a 2-1/2 year high on a trade-weighted basis, a 19-month peak against the dollar and a 22-month high against the mark.

"Sterling is a high yielding, liquid, low inflation currency backed up by a strong economy which is being actively encouraged to rise by the government and the central bank," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.
"There are no fears they are going to be intervening to slow the pace of the appreciation...I think it will continue further upwards."
The pound rose to $1.6348 and 2.4655 marks. Analysts said that given its strength against the dollar, it stood a chance of returning to its May 1994 high against the mark of 2.52.
Beyond that lies 2.62, the high reached in January 1994 after sterling recovered from the 1992 crisis when it was ejected from the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
"From a purely technical basis there is a chance we will get to 2.62 but I think 2.52 will cap it," said one trader.
On sterling/dollar there was a lot of upside resistance in the $1.61-63 area but the only big area of resistance is the top of the spike up to around $1.6575 in March 1995.

Traders said that has to be the target for cable, although it is 2-1/2 cents away and at present looks unattainable and other technical indicators like the 14-day relative strength index (RSI) make it already look overbought.

To some extent sterling was being underpinned by the expectation that Clarke would not give in to pressure from within his own party for a vote wining relaxation of monetary policy and raise rates ahead of the election next year.
"It's not only the expectation of interest rate rises that are supporting the pound now, it is the fact," said David Bloom, currency strategist a HSBC Markets.
"This means sterling is reasonably underpinned at current levels an if you believe he will put another quarter point on rates you could be looking at $1.68 and above."
The picture on cable is far more bullish than on sterling/mark because there much depends on what happens to German interest rates and dollar/mark.
Dollar/mark has been driving sterling/mark higher since early August and any big shake out would have a knock on effect.
But few in the market see the dollar sliding sharply against the German currency.

"There is the strong magnetic pull of round numbers so 2.50 on sterling/mark looks on the cards," said one trader. "The only thing which could scupper that would be a collapse of dollar/mark but the Bundesbank would not allow that."

Another thing which could hurt the pound would be complaints from British exporters about the uncompetitive level of sterling and high interest rates. But many big British companies contribute funds to the ruling Conservative party and a general election is only around six months away.
"You don't go to Conservative central office one day and give them half a million pounds and call the Chancellor an idiot the next day, do you?" said one trader.
"The newspapers and industry will applaud this move and sterling will firm further...Clarke is today's hero."
